header.tag_why: The evaluation started with store returns and split customer records, the decisive workshop was about stores, and we never showed an online order being returned at a till or produced a rollout plan; we also met the COO who signed only once.

messaging_changes.current_line: Online and in-store on one platform; the line between them has pretty much disappeared.
messaging_changes.change: For retail buyers with stores and a website, especially store operations leaders, replace the claim with the walkthrough and their words: 'One system for the tills and the website.' Then show it step by step: an online order is returned at the till, refunded to the original payment, and recorded on one customer record, so it's 'one customer, one basket.' Drop 'unified commerce', 'in-person payments' and 'point of sale' in this context, and say 'the tills'.
messaging_changes.why: The head of store ops dismissed the M3 unified-commerce section as 'a diagram' and asked right away how a return works at the till, while the customer's own phrasing was 'One system for the tills and the website' and 'one customer, one basket'.

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: For retail store rollouts, replace tiered support with single accountability and named people: 'One owner for your stores: we run the rollout and the installs under our name, with a named retail team that has done store rollouts.' Never present installs as 'a partner' handing off, because buyers have said 'I don't want two vendors pointing at each other.'
messaging_changes.why: The competitor reportedly brought 'people who'd done store rollouts', and our answer 'we'd bring in a partner' ended the store ops lead's questions because it failed the COO's stated criterion: 'I don't want two vendors pointing at each other.'

messaging_changes.change: Add a retail proof point set that sales can deploy on short notice: (1) a live demo of an online order being returned at a store till; (2) a sample store rollout plan covering dates, who installs, and what happens to the old tills; (3) reference retailers who will take a call quickly. Lead retail late-stage conversations with this proof instead of customer stories alone.
messaging_changes.why: The customer asked for three things: a reference call ('can I talk to them?'), a rollout plan ('Dates, who installs, what happens to the old tills'), and a live till return. We 'couldn't set up a call in time' and 'never showed' the return, while the competitor 'named retailers Angela knew'.

messaging_changes.change: Add an operations-led opener for retail deals with stores and a website, aimed at the COO and head of store operations as well as the CTO running the RFP. Start from the buy-online-return-in-store problem, where the store can't see the online order and loyalty breaks because store and web are 'two different customer records'. Lead with this before any checkout or wallet content.
messaging_changes.why: The evaluation was triggered by store returns and a loyalty program split across 'two different customer records', the deal was signed by the COO whom we met 'Once', and after the competitor's meeting the focus moved from web to 'it was stores'.

trigger.insight: The pain was operational and lived in the stores: returns at the till and a loyalty program broken by two customer records. Its origin story points to the COO, not the CTO. The rep knew this story, yet our engagement ran through the CTO's RFP and the early questions were all web. We sold checkout to a company that had come to us with a returns problem.
trigger.messaging: For omnichannel retail deals, open with the buy-online-return-in-store scenario and the single customer record, before any checkout or wallet content.

competitor.insight: We only have Raj's account of the Adyen meeting, and the rep was not there. By that account, Adyen won on who they brought (people with store rollout experience) and who they could name (retailers Angela knew), not on a feature list. The 11-of-14 question list is the hard signal. After meeting Adyen, the customer reframed the deal around stores, with questions such as 'Who shows up when a till goes down on a Saturday', and we stayed anchored on web.
competitor.messaging: Answer 'who shows up' directly: name the store rollout team and give till-down coverage, rather than offering a generic support tier (M5).

message.insight: The applause came from the ecommerce lead, who did not sign. The M3 line, 'the line between them has pretty much disappeared', was dismissed by the head of store ops as 'a diagram'. She immediately asked for the step-by-step return, which is the exact trigger scenario. M3 asserts the outcome without showing the mechanics, and to store operators an assertion reads as a vendor that hasn't done it.
message.messaging: Replace the M3 claim with a step-by-step walkthrough of an online order returned at the till, refunded to the original payment and recorded on one customer record.

gaps.insight: All three asks were requests for proof that we had done this before: a retailer to call, a rollout plan and a live return. None was a request for a new feature. The transcript does not establish whether we can do the till return today or why it wasn't demoed. Nothing indicates a rollout plan was ever delivered. A case study (M8) was not enough when the competitor was naming retailers the COO knew.
gaps.messaging: Build a ready-to-run retail proof kit: a live till-return demo, a sample store rollout plan covering dates, installer and old-till retirement, and reference retailers who will take a call on short notice.

language.insight: The customer framed the problem as one accountable system and one customer, in operator words: 'the tills', 'one customer, one basket'. We answered in category jargon such as 'unified commerce', 'in-person payments' and 'point of sale', which they never used. Angela's 'two vendors' line was a buying criterion, and our partner answer failed it.
language.messaging: Use their words in retail messaging: 'one system for the tills and the website' and 'one customer, one basket', plus a single-accountability promise, instead of 'unified commerce' and 'point of sale'.

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom: beyond Raj saying he wanted us, what evidence shows Raj's influence? Did anyone from our side try to reach Angela after the kickoff?

gaps.question: What did you say when Bev asked how a return works at the till?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom and the solutions engineer: can we actually run an online-order return at a store till today, and if so, why was it described rather than demoed?

gaps.question: What exactly did Adyen show or promise?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Raj, or Angela if reachable, in a loss interview: what did Adyen's retail team show, and which named retailers mattered?

gaps.question: Was a rollout plan ever delivered?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom: did we send a rollout plan with dates, installer and old-till handling, and if not, what blocked it?

gaps.question: Why couldn't a reference call be set up in time?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom and the customer reference team: which retail references exist, and what is the turnaround for a call?

gaps.question: What did they use before for tills and web?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom: who were the incumbent providers for store and online, and how did that shape the migration questions?

gaps.question: How much did 'one contract' weigh against price or terms?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom: did commercial terms or single-contract structure come up in the final decision?

close.rep_takeaway: Follow the trigger to its owner. This evaluation started with returns at a till, and the person who stood in that store signed the contract. When the problem lives in operations, get to the operations leader early. When a store team asks to see something, show it live and bring someone who has done a rollout. Describing it, or answering with 'a partner', tells them we haven't done it.
